worksheet.title: Forward and Back
worksheet.subtitle: Forward adds, back takes away
worksheet.learning_goal: I can run code that mixes forward and back blocks.

parts.title: Two kinds of moves
parts.text: A forward block moves Bit UP the path (it adds steps). A back block moves Bit DOWN the path (it takes steps away). Code can use both. Run the blocks in order, one at a time, to find where Bit lands.

parts.title: Run Code A
parts.prompt: Start on 1. Forward 3, then back 1. Run it one block at a time. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Predict, then run Code B
parts.prompt: PREDICT where Bit will land. Then run Code B from 3: forward 1, then back 2. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Build C — start at 2, reach 4
parts.note: Use ONE forward block and ONE back block.

parts.title: You try — mix the moves
parts.prompt: Fill the 2 empty blocks with one forward and one back block so Bit goes from 2 to 4. Run it to check. What did you use?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Forward adds steps and back takes steps away — just like adding and subtracting. Code can mix forward and back blocks to reach a number.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students run instructions that mix forward (add) and back (subtract) blocks, then write one of their own. Forward is like adding and back is like taking away — so coding the number line is doing math. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: Paper and pencil only. Optional: a floor number line 0 to 5 so students can step forward and back to feel adding and taking away.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them first (you do). Run Code A: "start at 1… forward 3 to 4… back 1 to 3." Name it: forward adds, back takes away.
2. Do one together (we do). Exercise 1: Code A lands on 3. Exercise 2: predict Code B, then run — forward 1 to 4, back 2 to 2.
3. Let them try alone (you do). Exercise 3: from 2, use one forward and one back block to reach 4 (e.g. forward 3, back 1).
4. Big idea: "Forward is like adding and back is like subtracting — coding the number line is doing math."

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Code A: 1 → forward 3 → 4 → back 1 → 3. Bit lands on 3.
Exercise 2 — Code B: 3 → forward 1 → 4 → back 2 → 2. Bit lands on 2.
Exercise 3 — start 2 → 4: e.g. forward 3, back 1 (a net of forward 2). Any forward/back pair that nets +2 works.
Why it works: each block runs in order; forward adds its number and back subtracts its number, so the landing is start + forwards − backs (kept on the 0–5 line).

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: treating a back block as forward. Point to the back word and step the wrong way once to contrast.
Make it easier: do Codes A and B only; skip the build task.
Make it harder: ask for a 2-to-4 answer that uses a back block first (e.g. back 1 to 1, then forward 3 to 4).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students follow (or write) step-by-step instructions, in order, to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions someone wrote, change one, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The student lands Code A on 3 and Code B on 2 and writes a forward+back answer that reaches 4.
